n: The righteous die and no one notices. Devout people are taken away, and no one realizes that God may be sparing them from coming evil. Death can be a mercy for the faithful.

f.w: the righteous is taken away from the evil to come

n: They enter peace and rest—those who lived uprightly. Latter-day revelation calls the spirit world for the righteous a paradise of rest.

f.g: Rest in their graves—death pictured as sleep.

n: God turns to the idolaters with harsh words: come here, children of a sorceress and of adultery. In the prophets, adultery is often a metaphor for unfaithfulness to the covenant.

f.g: A sharp insult: their spiritual “mother” is witchcraft.

n: Whom are you mocking—sticking out your tongues and sneering? You are children of rebellion and lies.
They inflame themselves with fertility rites under green trees and sacrifice children in the ravines—horrific practices linked to Molech worship that the law forbade.

f.w: slaying the children in the valleys

n: Their “portion” is the smooth stones of the stream—worshipped as idols—instead of the Lord, who should be their portion. Why would God be pleased with such offerings?

f.w: Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion
f.g: A wordplay: the Lord was meant to be Israel’s portion (inheritance), not stones.
A grain offering (meat = food in the KJV).

n: On high hills they set their “bed”—a picture of spiritual adultery at hilltop shrines.
They hid pagan symbols behind their doorposts—where God’s law was supposed to be written—and made covenants with idols. The image is of an unfaithful spouse.

f.w: Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance

f.g: Uncovered yourself—exposed yourself to another lover.

n: They went to “the king”—perhaps the god Molech, whose name resembles the Hebrew for king, or foreign kings—with oils and perfumes, sending envoys far and sinking even to Sheol.

f.g: Hebrew melek; possibly a play on Molech, the god of child sacrifice.
Hebrew Sheol—the underworld, the realm of the dead.

n: Worn out from chasing idols, they still wouldn’t admit it was hopeless. They found just enough strength to keep going, so they never felt sorry.
Whom were you so afraid of that you lied and forgot Me? Because God stayed quiet, they stopped fearing Him.

f.w: have not I held my peace even of old

n: God will expose their so-called righteousness and deeds—none of it will help them.

f.g: Sarcastic: “I’ll show what your ‘righteousness’ really is.”

n: When you cry for help, let your collection of idols save you—a breath of wind will blow them away. But whoever trusts in the Lord will inherit the land and His holy mountain.

f.w: he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land

n: A call goes out: build up the road, prepare the way, and remove every obstacle from the path of God’s people.

f.w: Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way

n: A treasured verse: the high and lofty One who lives in eternity, whose name is Holy, lives both in the highest heaven and with the humble and repentant, to revive their spirits. God’s greatness doesn’t keep Him distant from the broken-hearted.
God won’t accuse forever or stay angry always, or the human spirits He created would faint before Him. He knows our limits.

f.w: I will not contend for ever

n: Because of Israel’s greed, God was angry, struck them, and hid His face; yet they kept going stubbornly their own way.
Yet God says, “I have seen his ways, and I will heal him.” He will lead and comfort them, including those who mourn. Healing comes even to the undeserving.

f.w: I have seen his ways, and will heal him

n: God creates praise on people’s lips: “Peace, peace to the far and the near.” Paul applies this to Christ bringing peace to both Gentiles (far) and Jews (near).

f.w: Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near

n: But the wicked are like the stormy sea that can never be still, constantly churning up mud and filth.
“There is no peace for the wicked,” says God—echoing Isaiah 48:22 and closing this section.
